body.text:
What the hell are Fable, Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku?

These are the 4 model classes of @claudeai 

In order from MOST to LEAST intelligent, it’s:
Fable
Opus
Sonnet
Haiku

When should you use each?

Well, the more intelligent the model, the more complex of tasks it can handle, and the longer it can go without making a mistake. It also will tend to use more tokens, so if you want to save that, you can use a lower model or turn down the “effort” (this keeps the level of judgement high while ‘forcing’ Claude to do less ‘thinking’ and fewer tool calls.)

All 4 model classes can be used in Chat, Cowork, and Claude Code, AND they all have access to the same connectors and skills.

Hbu? Which model do you use the most? What other differences have you noticed?

Thanks to the team at @claudeai for helping bring this video to life.

I was confused as to why the break closest to my house was always wrong. I had heard CDM is a great wave but anytime I’m driving by, it’s flat. I wanted to understand exactly what was happening, because no forecast that I’ve seen has ever got it right. 

I think the difficulty in creating something like this is the level of detail that goes into every tiny piece. I have seen so many other apps pop up that just copy everyone else and claiming to be some new great addition to the world when they are clearly just in it for profit. 

I want to make the BEST surf forecasting app and I want to make it FREE. When Anthropic reached out saying they wanted to help me with the build, I knew it was actually possible. 

Do you have any spots that other forecasting apps get wrong all the time? If so let me know I’ll make sure I get it right.

body.text:
First, I keep choosing Claude Code for iOS because it’s THE BEST I’ve used for design and anything that requires exploration and creativity @claudeai #ClaudePartner

Even with Opus 5, I get better results for that kind of work than with anything else I’ve tried. And that’s before even getting into Fable 👀

Here’s my current workflow for building iOS apps:

• Opus 5 with ultracode when I’m building multiple features at the same time. Otherwise, Opus 5 on Max.

• Fable 5.1 on High for extremely complex issues. I rarely go above that.

I’m using Claude Code in the desktop app on a Mac, with Xcode installed.

Tell Claude to build your app and use the simulator to test it. The simulator opens inside Claude Code, and you can watch it tap through screens and check its work.

You can also switch between available devices and iOS versions, or interact with the app yourself.

For more specific build and testing workflows, you can connect tools like XcodeBuildMCP too.

I also use simulators for iPad and Apple Watch development. Lately I’ve been using them to work on my Apple Watch designs.

The most important part is giving Claude a clear goal AND telling it how to verify that it’s done.

For a larger feature, I use /goal and spell out:

• What needs to work.

• Which screens and interactions to test.

• What it shouldn’t change.

• What counts as finished.

Something like:

“Build [feature], then use the simulator to test [specific flows]. Fix anything that fails and test it again. Only mark the goal complete once those checks pass. If you’re blocked, tell me what’s stopping you.”

That gives Claude something concrete to keep working toward, so I’m not sitting there prompting every next step.

I still review the result, but having Claude run the app and check its own changes has been a really useful addition to my workflow.

You can try Claude Code on the Max plan through the link in my bio.

@claudeai #claudecode #iosdevelopment
